cues.text: A Despised Profession
Before his call, Matthew is traditionally identified with Levi, son of Alphaeus, who worked as a tax collector at Capernaum.
This position made him, in the eyes of his fellow Jews, something close to a traitor, since Roman tax-farming systems were widely and often justly associated with corruption.
Those who collected duties for a foreign power were classed together with public sinners and excluded from polite religious society.

Matthew, in other words, had built for himself a comfortable but deeply compromised life, secure in wealth but excluded from the very religious community whose Law he had, in his profession, effectively set aside.
"Follow Me"
Jesus's call to Matthew came with a directness that admits no elaboration.
Passing by the customs post, he said only, "follow me."
Matthew, Scripture tells us, rose and followed him, leaving behind, in that single instant, both his post and the income it represented, with no recorded hesitation or bargaining.
The speed of this response places Matthew's calling alongside the sudden, total abandonment of nets by Peter and Andrew.
This is proof that the summons of Christ, wherever and to whomever it comes, does not ask for a partial or negotiated response, but for everything, offered at once.
A Feast for Sinners
Matthew's first act as a new disciple reveals something of the man's own generous heart.
Rather than quietly slipping away from his old life, he was associated with a banquet at which Jesus ate with tax collectors and others regarded as sinners.
He invited tax collectors and others the religious establishment dismissed as sinners, so that they too might encounter the man who had called him.
When the Pharisees objected to Jesus dining with such disreputable company, he answered them with words that would become one of the clearest statements of his entire mission.
He said: those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick...
I came not to call the righteous, but sinners — a defense that Matthew, of all people, had every reason to treasure for the rest of his life.
The First Gospel
Ancient Christian tradition attributes the Gospel that bears Matthew's name to the Apostle Matthew.
Early testimony associated it with a Jewish-Christian setting, although its authorship, original form, and intended audience remain subjects of scholarly discussion.
and structured with careful attention to showing how Jesus fulfilled the Law and the Prophets of Israel's own Scriptures.
It was placed first in the New Testament's traditional ordering, though it is not the longest of the four Gospels.
That distinction belongs to Luke, while St. Augustine defended Matthew's position as fitting because it thoroughly bridges the Old Covenant and the New.
A former tax collector's practiced eye for careful record-keeping may well be reflected in the Gospel's methodical structure.
It contains five great blocks of teaching, including the Sermon on the Mount, interwoven with narrative.
Many scholars have found this pattern to be deliberately reminiscent of the five books of Moses.
A Mission Beyond Judea

Beyond the New Testament itself, tradition sends Matthew further afield to preach after Pentecost, with different accounts placing his later ministry and eventual martyrdom in Ethiopia, Persia, or Parthia.
The ancient world sometimes named these regions loosely and interchangeably, making the precise geography of his final years genuinely uncertain.
Even so, Christian tradition consistently remembers Matthew as a faithful missionary, although the circumstances and place of his death remain uncertain.
Legacy

Matthew's transformation—from a man whose very profession embodied collaboration and exploitation to an Apostle and Evangelist—remains one of the most complete pictures of conversion the New Testament offers.
The Gospel of Matthew has shaped Christian understanding of Jesus for two thousand years.
His story assures every believer who has ever felt too compromised, too far outside respectable religion, or too defined by past choices that Christ's call comes precisely to such places.
The same two words once spoken to a corrupt tax collector's booth in Capernaum — follow me — are spoken with equal directness.
They are spoken to every heart still willing to rise and leave the old life behind.
